source.title: The Spotlight Resonance Method: Resolving the Alignment of Embedded Activations

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses local coding and reports neuron-level alignment analyses, but it does not test whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how common polysemantic neurons are, or whether the claim's proposed explanations hold.
record.gate_note: The paper's SRM results measure alignment with privileged basis directions, and its selected-neuron analyses interpret category-dependent responses in image autoencoders. Those results do not measure polysemanticity as defined by any claim version. The paper also cites findings from other work, which are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study introduces the Spotlight-Resonance Method and shows that latent activations in MNIST/CIFAR autoencoders align with the privileged basis set by the activation function. It does not measure whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how common such neurons are, or what causes polysemanticity. Its hand-picked 'grandmother neuron' examples do show mixed class responses that the authors read as one shared feature, which resembles V6. But they are subjective, selected, from reconstruction autoencoders rather than classifiers, and not framed or measured as polysemanticity, so they do not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors' main conclusion is that the activation function's privileged basis causes the alignment: representations cluster around it, not around the standard basis, in all models tested. They present preliminary hand-picked examples of grandmother neurons and say these are present but not universal. They state this falls short of establishing local coding across the network.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces and applies Spotlight-Resonance and signed Spotlight-Resonance analyses; it does not reproduce the original studies' methods for identifying polysemantic neurons.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment results vary with the privileged basis and spotlight threshold; the paper reports that some networks require a lower epsilon to show a signal and that simplex-basis results can be anti-aligned.

fits_no_version.finding: Hand-picked privileged directions in trained MNIST and CIFAR reconstruction autoencoders show category-dependent signed alignment. The authors subjectively read these as single-concept detectors (scene/sky-water, vehicles/metal, eyes, digit hook shapes). They also say some neurons showed no such per-category variation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some selected latent neurons in fully connected image autoencoders respond across several labelled classes in a way that can be read as one shared human-interpretable feature. Such 'grandmother neurons' are present but not universal.

fits_no_version.finding: Latent representations align or anti-align with the privileged basis induced by the activation function, not with the standard basis when a rotated or non-standard basis is used.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron-basis alignment of representations is caused by the basis privileged by the activation function's functional form, rather than being innate to the standard basis.

record.peer_reviewed: To appear at the ICLR 2025 Workshop on Representational Alignment (Re-Align); arXiv.org
record.problems: The neuron interpretations are subjective and based on hand-picked directions. The paper says its local-coding results are preliminary and insufficient to establish local coding across the full network. The reported plots do not provide numerical uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. General SRM alignment plots were not recorded as rows because they measure alignment with a privileged basis, not polysemanticity or the claim versions' named behaviours.

untested.parts: Neurons in image classifiers (e.g. InceptionV1) responding to several unrelated inputs; only autoencoder latents were studied.
Prevalence of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer language models and how it varies by layer.
Superposition as the cause of polysemanticity; superposition is mentioned only speculatively.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization or noise without capacity pressure.
The share of polysemantic neurons as a function of activation function or architecture. The paper varies the activation basis but measures alignment, not polysemanticity.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons are really single-feature detectors, and how rare truly unrelated mixtures are.
Dependence of polysemanticity judgments on the activation range examined or on explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T6/discusses call and the 'none' links on all five rows are correct; states of cannot_determine are appropriate for figure-only, subjectively interpreted selected-neuron results. The authors' reading of mixed-class responses as single features superficially echoes V6. However, there is no polysemanticity measure, no unrelated-vs-related criterion and no prevalence count, and the models are reconstruction autoencoders, so no verdict is given.

versions.untested_parts: Whether image-classifier neurons respond strongly to several unrelated inputs, including the stated InceptionV1 example.
Language models, transformer MLP neurons, token or context polysemanticity, and layer differences.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or by representing more sparse features than neurons.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
The share of polysemantic neurons, its change with activation function or architecture, and any performance cost of reducing that share.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons are actually detectors of one shared feature or related jobs, and how often truly unrelated mixtures occur.
Whether polysemanticity depends on the activation range examined or on how explanations are scored.

rows.subject: large CIFAR network
rows.operation_detail: Applied signed spotlight resonance to a hand-picked privileged bivector and compared responses across CIFAR classes.
rows.measure: Signed spotlight-resonance pattern across labelled classes; authors interpret the direction as a scene detector associated with woodland versus sky and water.
rows.value: figure only; text reports strongest negative response for ships and aeroplanes, and positive response for several animal and vehicle classes
rows.locator: Appendix B.2, Figure 3 and accompanying text
rows.note: The paper calls the interpretation subjective and says the neuron appears to detect scenes. This is a selected-neuron analysis, not a test of how often unrelated response mixtures occur.

rows.subject: large CIFAR network
rows.operation_detail: Applied signed spotlight resonance to a hand-picked privileged bivector and compared responses across CIFAR classes.
rows.measure: Signed spotlight-resonance pattern across labelled classes; authors tentatively interpret the direction as related to mechanical vehicles or metal/grey, with negative responses to pets.
rows.value: figure only; text reports stronger positive responses for trucks, cars, aeroplanes and ships, and negative responses for dogs and cats
rows.locator: Appendix B.2, Figure 3 and accompanying text
rows.note: The proposed interpretation is subjective, and the paper says the direction is difficult to relate to the UMAP embedding.

rows.subject: large CIFAR network
rows.operation_detail: Applied signed spotlight resonance to a hand-picked privileged bivector and compared responses across CIFAR classes.
rows.measure: Signed spotlight-resonance pattern across labelled classes; authors tentatively interpret the direction as an eye-like feature detector.
rows.value: figure only; text reports strong negative response for aeroplanes and trucks and positive responses for several animal and vehicle classes
rows.locator: Appendix B.2, Figure 3 and accompanying text
rows.note: The interpretation is explicitly tentative and subjective; the paper says the direction does not clearly correspond to a direction in the UMAP plot.

rows.subject: large MNIST network
rows.operation_detail: Applied signed spotlight resonance to a hand-picked privileged bivector and compared responses across digit classes.
rows.measure: Signed spotlight-resonance pattern across digit classes; authors describe a response associated roughly with an upper-left-facing sharp or curved open shape.
rows.value: figure only; text orders the strongest positive responses as 1, then 7, 3, 2, followed by 5, 9, 4, 8, 0, and 6
rows.locator: Appendix B.2, Figure 4 and accompanying text
rows.note: The paper says the neuron's meaning is challenging to categorize; this is not a test of unrelated-input polysemanticity.

rows.subject: large MNIST network
rows.operation_detail: Applied signed spotlight resonance to a hand-picked privileged bivector and compared responses across digit classes.
rows.measure: Signed spotlight-resonance pattern across digit classes; authors interpret the direction as responding to the absence of a leftward hook shape.
rows.value: figure only; text reports stronger positive responses for 6, 0, 8, 4, 9, 5 and 2, with little activation for 7 or 1
rows.locator: Appendix B.2, Figure 4 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors describe this as opposite in ordering to the other selected MNIST direction. It does not establish the prevalence or nature of polysemantic neurons.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
